```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5)
```

`nlestim` fits nonlinear regression models by Gauss-Newton or
Levenberg-Marquardt and gives you everything needed to report the result. This
vignette shows the workflow on the bundled data; replace the data frame and
column names with your own.

```{r}
library(nlestim)
```

## 1. The one-call workflow

`nl_workflow()` takes a data frame and the names of the x and y columns. It
chooses candidate models from the shape of the data, fits them, ranks them by
AICc and reports the best one with profile-likelihood confidence intervals.

```{r}
wf <- nl_workflow(plant_growth, x = "day", y = "biomass")
wf
```

The figure shows every candidate curve, the best fit with 95% confidence and
prediction bands, and residual diagnostics:

```{r, fig.height = 6}
plot(wf)
```

The Gompertz curve wins. That is correct: these data were simulated from a
Gompertz curve. The logistic curve looks almost as good by eye, but its residual sum of
squares is about 50% larger, which AICc reflects.

### Choosing the candidate models yourself

```{r}
nl_models()[, c("model", "formula")]
nl_workflow(crop_yield_nitrogen, "nitrogen", "yield",
            models = c("asymptotic_regression", "michaelis_menten", "logistic"),
            plot = FALSE)$comparison
```

### Saving everything for a report

Give an `output_dir` and the workflow writes the comparison table, parameter
tables, fitted values, a prediction curve with bands, a PNG figure and a
plain-text report:

```{r}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "yield-analysis")
wf <- nl_workflow(crop_yield_nitrogen, "nitrogen", "yield", output_dir = out, plot = FALSE)
basename(wf$files)
```

## 2. Your own data

Read a CSV or Excel file with `nl_read()` (Excel needs the readxl package), then
run the workflow on the columns you need:

```{r}
path <- system.file("extdata", "dose_response.csv", package = "nlestim")
my_data <- nl_read(path)
names(my_data)
names(my_data) <- c("conc", "viability")
nl_workflow(my_data, "conc", "viability", plot = FALSE)$parameters
```

Every bundled dataset comes with a ready-made call:

```{r}
nl_datasets()[, c("dataset", "kind", "n", "workflow")]
```

## 3. Fitting a single model

With a built-in model, starting values are automatic:

```{r}
fit <- nl_fit(rate ~ conc, puromycin, model = "michaelis_menten")
summary(fit)
```

Or write any formula, exactly as with `stats::nls()`. Derivatives are taken
analytically with `deriv()`:

```{r}
fit2 <- nl_fit(rate ~ Vmax * conc / (Km + conc), puromycin,
               start = c(Vmax = 200, Km = 0.1), method = "gn")
coef(fit2)
```

## 4. Inference

Wald intervals assume the model is close to linear in each parameter.
Profile-likelihood intervals follow the real shape of the sum of squares, and
bootstrap intervals make no such assumption:

```{r}
confint(fit)                       # Wald
confint(fit, method = "profile")   # profile likelihood (as R's confint for nls)
confint(fit, method = "bootstrap", R = 500)
```

The profile t plot shows why the Km interval is asymmetric:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
pr <- nl_profile(fit, "Km")
plot(pr$value, pr$tau, type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "Km", ylab = "profile t",
     main = "Curved profile: Wald intervals are only approximate")
abline(h = c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, df.residual(fit)), lty = 3)
abline(a = -coef(fit)["Km"] / sqrt(vcov(fit)["Km", "Km"]),
       b = 1 / sqrt(vcov(fit)["Km", "Km"]), col = "grey50", lty = 2)
```

## 5. Prediction, comparison and weights

```{r}
predict(fit, data.frame(conc = c(0.05, 0.5)), interval = "prediction")

full <- nl_fit(yield ~ nitrogen, crop_yield_nitrogen, model = "asymptotic_regression")
reduced <- nl_fit(yield ~ a * (1 - exp(-c * nitrogen)), crop_yield_nitrogen,
                  start = c(a = 10, c = 0.01))
anova(reduced, full)   # is the yield without nitrogen really above zero?
```

When the noise grows with the response (constant coefficient of variation),
weight each point by `1 / fitted^2`:

```{r}
f0 <- nl_fit(conc ~ time, drug_elimination, model = "exponential_decay")
fw <- nl_fit(conc ~ time, drug_elimination, model = "exponential_decay",
             weights = 1 / fitted(f0)^2)
rbind(unweighted = coef(f0), weighted = coef(fw))
```
